parole.significato: An expression of approval; praise.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1591 in the publications of Thomas Lodge, borrowed from French accolade, from Occitan acolada (“an embrace”), from acolar (“to embrace”), from Italian accollato, via Vulgar Latin *accollō (“to hug around the neck”), from Latin ad- + collum (“neck”) (English collar) + -āta.

parole.significato: The sun-facing side of a mountain; in the northern hemisphere, this is typically the south-facing slope.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French adret or Occitan adret, adré, adrech, adreit (“sun-facing side of a mountain”), from Old Occitan adreg, adreit, from a (“to, towards”) (from Latin ad (“to, towards”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“at; to”)) + dreg, dreit (“just; right”) (from Latin dīrēctus (“direc

parole.significato: A type of sauce made from garlic and olive oil, often with egg and lemon juice and similar to mayonnaise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aïoli, from Occitan alhòli, from alh (“garlic”) + òli (“oil”).

parole.significato: Playful raillery; banter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French badinage, from the verb badiner (“jest, joke”) from badin (“playful”), from Occitan badar (“gape”). Distantly related to abash.

parole.significato: A member of a cultural and ethnic people living in the western Pyrenees and the Bay of Biscay between France and Spain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Basque, from Gascon Occitan basc, from Latin Vascō, Vascōnēs pl, a pre-Roman era tribe settled in the Atlantic Biscaian gulf and Pyrenean mountain region of south-western Europe, who were ancestors of the current Basque population.

parole.significato: A mansion in Provence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bastide, from Occitan.

parole.significato: A type of round, brimless cap with a soft top and a headband to secure it to the head; usually culturally associated wi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French béret, from Occitan (Gascon) berret (“cap”), from Old Occitan berret, from Medieval Latin birretum, from Late Latin birrus (“large hooded cloak”), from Gaulish birrus (“short cloak”), from Proto-Celtic *birros (“short”) (compare Welsh byr, Middle Irish berr). Compare biretta.

parole.significato: A demijohn or carboy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bonbonne f, from Occitan boumbouno m [from boumbo + -ouno, ultimately from Latin bombus and -ōnem], made feminine in French under the influence of French bonne (unrelated), and with change of bomb- to bonb- under the influence of French bonbon (also unrelated). Although less com

parole.significato: A type of fish soup or stew from Provence, France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bouillabaisse, from Occitan bolhabaissa, bouiabaisso, possibly a compound of bolhir (“to boil”) + abaissar (“to lower (the temperature)”).

parole.significato: A puree of salted cod, olive oil, and milk.
parole.testo: From French brandade, from Occitan brandada, from brandar (“to stir”). Cognate to Spanish brandada.

parole.significato: An open chair mounted to one side of a pack animal, balanced by another on the other side.
parole.testo: From French cacolet, from Béarnais Occitan cacoulet (“mule chair”).

parole.significato: Describing a brand representing the most luxurious or highest quality example in its class. (derived from the GM car br…
parole.testo: From French Cadillac, from Occitan Cadilhac. Most places or objects named Cadillac are named for Antoine Laumet de La Mothe, sieur de Cadillac, a French explorer who founded the eponymous city in Maine and later the city of Detroit, Michigan.

parole.significato: A member of a persecuted minority in south-western France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cagot, from Occitan cagot, of uncertain origin, traditionally speculated to be connected to the Visigoths; according to modern postulation, possibly equivalent to cagar (“to defecate”) + -ot (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: A Provençal diamond-shaped confection made with ground almonds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French calisson, from Occitan calissoun.

parole.significato: A roughly conical earthenware vessel, glazed inside, used in cooking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cassole, from Occitan caçòla.

parole.significato: A rich stew originating in southwest France containing beans and meat.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French cassoulet, from Occitan caçolet.

parole.significato: A place above ground for storing wine casks.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chai, from Occitan.

parole.significato: A genre of riddles where the clues to the answer are descriptions or puns on its syllables, with a final clue to the wh…
parole.testo: From French charade, charrade (“prattle, idle conversation; a kind of riddle”), probably from Occitan charrada (“conversation; chatter”), from charrar (“to chat; to chatter”) + -ada. As a round of the game, originally a clipping of acting charade but now usually understood and formed as a back-forma

parole.significato: The earliest known form of modern human (Homo sapiens) in Europe, dating from the late Paleolithic.
parole.testo: From French Cro-Magnon, from Occitan Cròs-Manhon. Named after Abri de Cro-Magnon, a rock shelter in the commune of Les Eyzies-de-Tayac-Sireuil, Dordogne, France, where the first skeletons were found in 1868.

parole.significato: A lively chain dance in 6/8 time, of Provençal origin.
parole.testo: From French farandole, from Occitan farandola.

parole.significato: A member of a literary fellowship founded in 1854 to promote the literature and culture of Provence in France; also som…
parole.testo: From French félibre, from Occitan felibre.

parole.significato: A type of low scrubland found on limestone soils in southern France and other parts of the Mediterranean Basin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French garrigue, from Occitan.

parole.significato: Synonym of Languedocian
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Languedoc, from the univerbation of langue d'oc (“the language of oc”), from Dante Alighieri’s De vulgari eloquentia, where he wrote in Latin: “nam alii oc, alii si, alii vero dicunt oil” (‘some say òc, others say sì, others say oïl’). Based on the Occitan word òc (“yes”), in co

parole.significato: Alfalfa.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French luzerne, from Occitan luzerno, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: A country cottage or farmstead in Occitan-speaking territories.
parole.testo: From French mas, from Occitan mas, from Latin mānsum, from mānsus, perfect participle of maneō (“stay, remain, abide”). Doublet of manse.

parole.significato: Something thought to bring good luck.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mascotte, from Occitan mascòta (“sortilege”), feminine diminutive of masca (“witch”), from Old Occitan masca, from Medieval Latin masca (“specter, nightmare”). More at mask.

parole.significato: A mixture of small, young leaves as a salad
parole.testo: From French mesclun, from Occitan.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Nice.
parole.testo: From French nissard, from Occitan niçard. Compare Italian nizzardo.

parole.significato: A mixture consisting of egg white and a sweetener, variously mixed with (in western Europe) almonds or (in eastern Euro…
parole.testo: From French nougat, from Occitan nogat, from noga (“nut”), ultimately from Latin nux (“nut”) + -atus (“-ate, forming adjectives and substantives having or resembling some thing or trait”). Compare Spanish nuégado.

parole.significato: A small coin of the value of six-and-a-quarter cents; a Spanish coin with a value of half a real; a fippenny bit.
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from southern French picaillon, pécaillon, picayon (“type of small foreign coin; (informal, especially in the plural) cash, money”), and from its etymon Occitan picalhon, picaioun (“cheaply made Savoyan-Piedmontese coin that was rapidly demonetized; (by extension) cash, money”),

parole.significato: A traditional French Provençal stewed vegetable dish consisting primarily of tomatoes, zucchini and eggplant.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French ratatouille, from Occitan ratatolha (ratatouille is a dish originally from Nice, and is also found in Provence), French form from diminutive prefix tat- + touiller (“to stir”), from Latin tudiculō (“grind, mix”), from tudes (“hammer”), from Proto-Indo-European *tud-,

parole.significato: A blood dish from rural Occitania made immediately upon exsanguination of livestock by collecting, preparing, and cooki…
parole.testo: From French sanguette, from Occitan sanqueta.

parole.significato: A female attendant or servant, especially one who is cheeky or mischievous, often featuring in theatrical comedies.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French soubrette, from Occitan soubreta (“coy”) (feminine of soubret), from soubra (Provençal sobrar), from Latin superare (“be above”).

parole.significato: truffade (Occitan potato dish)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French truffade, from Occitan trufada.

parole.significato: Château d'Yquem, a prestigious wine produced in Sauternes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French, itself from Occitan Iquem, variant of Eiquem (French: Eyquem), from Latin Achelmus/Aichelmus, ultimately from Germanic.
